title: L1 · Intro to A&P
subtitle: Levels of organization, body systems, directions, homeostasis

lines.text: **Anatomy** is the study of structure.
It names the parts and regions of the body.
**Physiology** is the study of function.
It explains how the parts work together.
We learn them together because structure determines function.
Think of a spoon, a fork and a knife. Each shape does a different job.
The body is built in levels. Each level builds on the one before.
**Atoms** join into molecules. Molecules build macromolecules.
Macromolecules build **organelles**, the tiny organs inside a cell.
The **cell** is the smallest unit of life. Its study is cytology.
Similar cells form a **tissue**. Its study is histology.
Two or more tissues form an **organ**. Organs form an organ system.
All the systems together make the **organism**. That's you.
There are four tissue types.
**Epithelial**, **connective**, **muscle** and **nervous**.
Every organ is built from these four.
You will meet each one again in Lecture 5 and beyond.
The body has **eleven** organ systems.
The **integumentary** system is the skin, hair, glands and nails. Skin is the largest organ.
The **skeletal** system supports, protects, stores minerals like calcium and makes blood cells.
The **muscular** system moves the body by contraction.
The **nervous** system controls the body fast, with sensory input, integration and motor output.
The **endocrine** system controls the body more slowly, with hormones in the blood.
The **cardiovascular** system moves gases, nutrients and wastes, and helps regulate temperature.
The **lymphatic** system drains fluid and defends the body. It complements the cardiovascular system.
The **respiratory** system exchanges gases and helps regulate pH.
The **digestive** system takes in food, digests it, absorbs nutrients and gets rid of waste.
The **urinary** system filters nitrogen waste and regulates blood pressure, pH and water and salt balance.
The **reproductive** system produces offspring.
Every direction is described from **anatomical position**.
Standing upright. Feet forward. Arms at the sides. Palms facing forward.
Your client's right is never the same side as your right.
**Superior** means toward the head. Inferior means toward the feet.
**Anterior** means front. Posterior means back.
**Medial** means toward the midline. Lateral means away from it.
**Proximal** means close to the point of attachment. Distal means farther away.
**Superficial** means toward the surface. Deep means away from it.
Regional terms name body areas.
**Brachial** is the arm. Antebrachial is the forearm.
**Antecubital** is the front of the elbow. Olecranal is the back.
Patellar is the front of the knee. **Popliteal** is the back.
Sural is the calf. Calcaneal is the heel. **Plantar** is the sole of the foot.
Pollex is the thumb. Hallux is the big toe.
A **sagittal** plane divides the body into left and right.
Midsagittal divides it into equal halves.
A **coronal**, or frontal, plane divides front from back.
A **transverse** plane divides top from bottom.
An oblique plane cuts at an angle.
Cavities protect organs and let them change size and shape.
The **dorsal** cavity holds the brain and spinal cord.
The **ventral** cavity is the largest.
The **diaphragm** separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity.
The **mediastinum** sits in the middle of the chest. It encloses the heart, trachea and esophagus.
Four quadrants are centered on the navel.
**Right upper quadrant**: liver and gallbladder.
Right lower: the appendix.
**Left upper**: stomach and spleen. Left lower: sigmoid colon.
Nine regions form a tic-tac-toe grid.
The middle column, top to bottom, is **epigastric**, **umbilical**, hypogastric.
**Homeostasis** is a stable internal environment.
A feedback system has four parts.
The **stimulus** is a change from normal.
The **receptor** senses it and signals the control center.
The **control center** decides and sends instructions.
The **effector** responds. It is always a cell, tissue or organ.
In **negative feedback**, the response opposes the change. Most feedback is negative.
An ice cube cools the skin. Krause bulbs sense the cold.
The hypothalamus responds. Vessels constrict and muscles shiver.
Blood sugar rises after cake. Beta cells release **insulin**, and sugar falls.
Blood sugar drops. Alpha cells release **glucagon**, and sugar rises.
In **positive feedback**, the response amplifies the change.
It is natural but rare.
In childbirth, the cervix stretches and the pituitary releases **oxytocin**.
Contractions get stronger, which stretches the cervix more.
Blood **clotting** is the other classic example.
